Where is Benton, Arkansas, and what is the city like?

Benton is the county seat of Saline County and a suburb in the Little Rock-North Little Rock-Conway metro area. It sits at about 472 feet of elevation, and the Saline County Courthouse stands downtown.

The city's roots go back to the 1830s. It was named for Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton, and early industry included a salt works that opened in 1827, kaolin pottery from about 1900, and logging and furniture making from the surrounding timber. Those older trades explain why parts of town have small mid-century frame houses next to newer subdivisions.

Growth has been steady for decades. The Census Bureau count for Benton went from 21,906 in 2000 to 30,681 in 2010 and 35,014 in 2020, with a July 2025 estimate of 38,898. In 2020 the city had 14,785 housing units, and 7.1 percent were vacant.

Saline County itself had 123,416 residents in 2020 and covers about 730 square miles, with Bryant, Bauxite, Alexander and Shannon Hills among its other communities.

What does the climate mean for a Benton house?

Benton has a humid subtropical climate, so the main wear on a house comes from heat, moisture and rain rather than snow. The July mean daily high is about 92.9 degrees Fahrenheit, and the record high is 112 degrees. January lows average near 30.6 degrees.

With roughly 53 inches of rain a year and about 74 days of measurable precipitation, buyers and appraisers look hard at a few things:

  • Roof condition and past leaks, since long wet seasons find weak flashing.
  • Crawl space moisture, soft wood and sagging floors.
  • Air conditioner age, because summers are long and hot.
  • Gutters, grading and drainage around the foundation.

If your Benton house has any of these problems, a repair list can slow a conventional sale. Cash buyers who purchase as-is do not ask you to fix them first.

Which school districts serve Benton?

Most of Benton is served by the Benton School District, which feeds Benton High School. Other districts touch the area, so the address matters.

  • Benton School District: serves most of the city.
  • Bryant Public Schools: runs Bryant High School and serves nearby addresses.
  • Bauxite School District: covers the Bauxite area in the county.
  • Harmony Grove School District: serves a small area near Frontage Road in the southeast, with Benton Harmony Grove High School.

Confirm the district for a specific street before you advertise a house, since buyers with children usually ask. A house on a district boundary can pull different buyers than one a few blocks away.

What city rules and permits affect selling a house in Benton?

Benton's Community Development office handles building permits and code enforcement from City Hall at 410 River Street. The office posts forms for residential remodels, accessory buildings, swimming pools, fences, retaining walls, grading, demolition and house moving, and it also lists floodplain forms.

Code enforcement covers overgrown lots, standing water, and abandoned or inoperable vehicles. The city says boats, trailers, farm implements and vehicles may not stay on public property more than seven consecutive days unless they are inside a building or tied to a licensed business, and it treats such violations as public nuisances. You can reach the office at 501-776-5938, and permit submissions go to permits@bentonar.gov. Hours are Monday to Friday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.

Before listing, it helps to check for:

  • Open permits or unpermitted additions, decks and carports.
  • Code complaints for tall grass or stored vehicles.
  • Whether the lot sits in a mapped flood area, which would involve the floodplain forms.

A house with unresolved violations or work done without a permit can raise questions at inspection. Selling for cash as-is removes the need to cure those items yourself, though you should still disclose what you know.

How do property taxes work when you sell a house in Benton?

Saline County bills real estate tax one year behind, and the owner of record on the assessment date receives the bill. The county collector accepts payment from March 1 through October 15, and mailed payments must be postmarked by October 15. State law adds a 10 percent penalty to balances still unpaid after that date.

The collector's offices are in Benton and Bryant, open weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the main number is 501-303-5620. State law also lets taxpayers pay in installments: one quarter by the third Monday in April, another quarter by the third Monday in July, and the final half by October 15.

A reappraisal is under way. Saline County says notices began arriving in July 2026 and go only to owners whose values rose. They are not tax bills, and the new values will not show up in this October's payment. Owners who disagree contact the assessor first, then the county equalization board.

At closing, the contract and the settlement statement decide how the year's bill is split between seller and buyer, so ask the title company to show the tax line. Arkansas also charges a state real property transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of the sale price on transfers above $100. The Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration page for that tax does not say who must pay, so the purchase contract controls. See the state transfer tax page for details.

Getting around: where Benton sits for commuters and buyers

Saline County is crossed by Interstate 30 and its Business Loop, Interstate 530, U.S. Highways 65, 67, 70 and 167, and Arkansas Highways 5, 9 and 35. That road network is part of why the city works as a bedroom community for Little Rock workers.

Commute access shapes who buys. People who commute to Little Rock look at Benton because it is a county seat with its own downtown. If your house is close to an interchange or a main road, mention it plainly in any listing or cash-offer conversation.

What do sellers in Benton usually run into?

Sellers here tend to deal with the same few situations. A parent's house may have passed to several heirs. A rental may have tenants and deferred repairs. Some owners fall behind on a mortgage or tax bill, and others simply want to move without a round of showings.

Each path has a different timeline. A traditional listing means repairs, showings, a buyer's lender and an appraisal. A cash sale to an investor can close on a date you choose, and the buyer takes the house with its repairs. Compare the net amounts and the timing on both before you decide.

The Arkansas homestead credit, available to owner-occupants, is worth knowing about if you are still living in the house. The Benton County assessor describes the statewide credit as up to $600 off the tax bill on a primary residence. Saline County's assessor can confirm how it applies to your house.

More questions about Benton, AR

Is Benton the county seat of Saline County?

Yes. Benton is the county seat of Saline County, Arkansas, and the Saline County Courthouse is in its downtown. Deeds for Benton houses are recorded with the county.

When are Saline County property taxes due?

The deadline is October 15. The collector takes payments from March 1 through October 15, and a 10 percent penalty applies to unpaid balances after that date. Mailed payments need an October 15 postmark.

Do I need a permit or inspection to sell my Benton house?

A permit is not something this page can say is required for the sale itself, but any work done on the house should have been permitted. Benton's Community Development office issues permits for remodels, fences, pools and similar work. Ask them at 501-776-5938 if you are unsure about past work.

Can I sell a Benton house with code violations?

Yes. You can sell a house that has violations such as overgrown grass or stored vehicles, but open code issues can complicate a conventional sale. A cash buyer who buys as-is will usually take the house in its current condition. Contact Benton code enforcement to learn what is open on your address.

Which school district is my Benton house in?

Most addresses are in the Benton School District, but some fall in Bryant, Bauxite or Harmony Grove. Check the district for your exact street before you list or discuss the house with a buyer.

What is the Arkansas transfer tax on a house sale?

The state tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of the sale price on transfers over $100. For a $100,000 sale that is $330. The state page does not say who pays, so your contract and settlement statement decide.

Where is Bentonville, Arkansas, and how did it grow?

Bentonville is the county seat of Benton County in the northwest corner of Arkansas, with Rogers to the east, Bella Vista to the north and Centerton to the west. It is one of four main cities in the three-county Northwest Arkansas metro, which had 546,725 residents in 2020.

The town was incorporated on April 3, 1873, and was first called Osage before it took the name of Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton. The first railroad bypassed it and created Rogers instead, and in 1883 a local railroad company linked the two towns. In 1950 Sam Walton bought the Harrison Variety Store on the square, and Walton's 5 & 10 opened on March 18, 1951. That store led to Walmart.

The population shows how fast things changed: 19,730 in 2000, 35,301 in 2010, 54,164 in 2020 and an estimate of 63,057 for 2025. In 2020 the city counted 22,436 housing units, with 8.7 percent vacant.

Who employs people in Bentonville?

Walmart is the largest employer in Bentonville, and its Home Office is a campus of more than 20 buildings, mostly along Walton Boulevard (US 71B) on the west side. A consolidated headquarters on about 350 acres was announced in 2017, and the first part opened in January 2025. Over 1,100 vendors keep sales offices in the region to serve the company.

  • Walmart Inc.
  • Northwest Health System
  • Mercy of Northwest Arkansas
  • Bentonville School District
  • Benton County and the City of Bentonville
  • Northwest Arkansas Community College
  • Arvest Bank Group

For sellers, a job tied to one of these employers can mean a firm move date. A seller on a company schedule may not want to wait through a long listing period, which is when a quick as-is sale gets considered.

What is the climate like, and how does it affect a Bentonville house?

Bentonville has four distinct seasons under a humid subtropical climate with some continental influence. July averages a high of 89 degrees and a low of 66, while January averages a high of 46 and a low of 24. The record low is minus 16 degrees, set in 1996.

Snowfall averages 9.5 inches a year, and total precipitation is about 47 inches. Winter cold matters for heating and pipes. The county also sits on the Springfield Plateau, a karst landscape of springs, sinkholes and caves, which makes drainage and ground conditions worth checking.

Inspectors and buyers in this part of Arkansas tend to look at:

  • Roof age and storm damage.
  • Foundation movement and drainage on sloped lots.
  • Furnace and heat pump condition after cold stretches.
  • Sinkhole or ground-settlement signs on karst terrain.

Which school districts serve Bentonville addresses?

Bentonville Public Schools serve most of the city, with Bentonville High School and Bentonville West High School, the latter located in Centerton. Small eastern portions of the city are zoned to Rogers Public Schools.

Families also look at Haas Hall Academy and Founders Classical Academy, which are public charter schools, and at the independent Thaden School, which opened in 2017. Northwest Arkansas Community College is the public two-year college. Zoning can differ from one street to the next, so check the district for an exact address before you describe a house to a buyer.

Roads, airport and trails

Interstate 49, which carries US 71 and was redesignated from I-540 on March 28, 2014, is the main route through Bentonville. The Bella Vista Bypass to the north opened in late 2021. Northwest Arkansas National Airport is about 12 miles southwest and opened in 1998, and Bentonville Municipal Airport (Louise M. Thaden Field) serves general aviation.

The city has more than 50 miles of trails, including a stretch of the 36-mile Razorback Regional Greenway and over 28 miles of mountain bike trails. The Crystal Bridges Trail runs about a mile from downtown to the museum.

How are property taxes and assessments handled for a Bentonville sale?

Benton County's collector opens the tax books on the first business day of March, and a 10 percent penalty applies to unpaid amounts after October 15. Taxes are paid one year behind, so a 2026 assessment is billed in 2027 and due October 15, 2027. The county says tax statements must be mailed by July 1.

The Benton County assessor explains that when real property sells, it is assessed at 20 percent of appraised value at the next assessment date after title transfers. A new owner cannot claim an assessed-value limitation until the second assessment date after the transfer. The county's next countywide reappraisal is listed as 2028. The homestead credit is up to $600 for a primary residence, and the assessor's homestead department is at 479-271-1037.

Tax bills go to the owner of record on January 1 of the tax year. The closing documents explain how buyer and seller split the bill. Card payments to the collector carry a convenience fee set by a service provider, with a $3.99 minimum for payments under $110 and 3.59 percent above that. Details are on the Benton County Collector FAQ. Arkansas also levies a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transfers over $100.

What permits and city offices matter when selling in Bentonville?

Building permits in Bentonville come from the Building and Fire Safety Division of the Fire Department, at 305 SW A Street. It issues building, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, moving, demolition, sign, pool, fire alarm, fire sprinkler and fence permits, and it issues certificates of occupancy once final inspection passes.

The office can be reached at 479-271-3108 or buildingpermits@bentonville.ar.gov, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. It also inspects substandard buildings. If you have a house with unpermitted work or an older structure with open questions, ask the division what is on record before you list.

The city has more than 30 properties on the National Register of Historic Places, including two historic districts. Owners of older houses near the square should check whether a house sits inside one, because it can change what repairs and exterior changes are practical for a buyer.

What do Bentonville sellers face when they need to sell quickly?

Many sellers in Bentonville are balancing a job move, an inheritance, a rental that did not work out, or a house that needs work. Whatever the pace of the market, a listing still involves repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal.

A cash purchase offers a different route: a single buyer, no financing contingency and a closing date you can pick. It is worth comparing against a listing, including what you would net after repairs and carrying costs. Ask for any offer in writing before you decide.

Is Bentonville the county seat of Benton County?

Yes. Bentonville is the seat of Benton County, and the 19th Judicial Circuit Court sits in the Benton County Courthouse. Deeds for Bentonville houses are recorded in the county.

When are Benton County property taxes due?

October 15 is the cutoff, with a 10 percent penalty after that date. The collector opens the books on the first business day of March. Taxes are billed one year behind the assessment year.

How does a sale change my property tax assessment in Bentonville?

The assessor reappraises the house at 20 percent of appraised value at the next assessment date after the title transfer. The new owner cannot claim an assessed-value limitation until the second assessment date after the transfer.

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell?

The city's building page does not say one is required for a resale. The Building and Fire Safety Division issues certificates of occupancy after construction is complete and final inspection is passed. Call 479-271-3108 if you are unsure about work done on your house.

Which district is my Bentonville house in?

Most of the city is in Bentonville Public Schools. Small eastern areas are zoned to Rogers Public Schools. Confirm the district for your address.

How far is Bentonville from the airport?

Northwest Arkansas National Airport is about 12 miles southwest of the city. It opened in 1998.

Where is Cabot, Arkansas, and what is its history?

Cabot is the largest city in Lonoke County, in the northwest part of the county, and it belongs to the Little Rock-North Little Rock-Conway metro area. It began in 1873 as a refueling stop on the Cairo and Fulton Railroad after the line bypassed nearby Austin, and it was incorporated on November 9, 1891.

Growth came in waves. The 1955 opening of Little Rock Air Force Base in Jacksonville brought families, and federal desegregation orders for the Little Rock School District in 1972 sent more to surrounding towns. Cabot's census population rose from 1,321 in 1960 to 8,319 in 1990, 15,261 in 2000, 23,776 in 2010 and 26,569 in 2020. The 2025 estimate is 27,711.

One event still shapes the downtown layout. A tornado struck Cabot on March 29, 1976, killing five people and destroying several buildings, and City Plaza was built on the rebuilt site. City Hall, the municipal courtroom and the police station now sit there.

How does the highway and Air Force Base connection affect Cabot housing?

Cabot sits along Interstate 57 and U.S. 67 and 167, a four-lane freeway on the northwest side of the city that leads about 22 miles southwest to Little Rock. Searcy is 26 miles northeast, and Jacksonville is 9 miles southwest on the same route.

That route links Cabot to two big sources of buyers. Many residents commute to Little Rock, and the city is described as a commuter town. Little Rock Air Force Base in Jacksonville is the other draw: about 40 percent of its military personnel are reported to live in Cabot, and the school district holds a Purple Star designation for supporting military families.

  • A seller with orders or a job transfer may care more about a firm closing date than a long listing period.
  • Distance to the freeway and to Jacksonville or Little Rock is a fact worth stating up front.

What is the climate in Cabot, and what does it do to a house?

Cabot has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mild to cool winters. The July mean high is 92.4 degrees and the January mean high is 51.2 degrees, with a record high of 112 degrees and a record low of minus 7. The city gets about 53 inches of precipitation over roughly 92 days a year, and about 2 inches of snow.

The 1976 tornado is a reminder that severe weather is part of life here. Buyers and appraisers commonly ask about:

  • Roof age, shingle condition and prior storm claims.
  • Windows, doors and garage doors that have taken wind damage.
  • Moisture in attics, crawl spaces and slabs after wet seasons.
  • Cooling system age.

Damage you have not repaired does not have to hold up a sale. A buyer who purchases as-is will price the work instead of asking you to finish it.

Which schools serve Cabot?

Cabot Public Schools serve Cabot, Austin and Ward, plus most of northern Lonoke County. The district includes Cabot High School and Cabot Junior High School North, which was rebuilt after a fire on August 10, 2006 destroyed the old building. No one was hurt in that fire.

Because the district reaches beyond city limits, a mailing address that says Cabot does not always mean the same district boundary. Check the school assignment for the specific parcel before you list or discuss it with a buyer.

What permits and city offices matter when you sell in Cabot?

Cabot's Planning and Zoning department at 1 City Plaza, Suite A handles residential permits and the zoning map. The city lists permits for additions and remodels, decks, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work, swimming pools, water heater replacement, generators, roofs, solar panels, sprinkler systems, storage buildings, sun rooms, porch enclosures and retaining walls.

The city's page says homeowners may do many repairs themselves but still need permits and must follow code, and it says that contractors should have purchased the permit for the work. The page says the work requires one or more inspections depending on the job.

Planning and Zoning can be reached at 501-843-4819. The city's GIS map has a zoning layer and the city recommends checking it before applying for a planning permit.

Before listing, look back at any work done on the house: a new roof, a deck, a water heater or an accessory building. If a permit was never pulled, ask the department what to do. A cash buyer will usually take a house that way, though you should tell them what you know.

How are property taxes handled for a house sale in Cabot?

Arkansas real property tax is due between the first business day of March and October 15 of the year after the levy, and the collector adds a 10 percent penalty to balances left after October 15. Cabot properties are billed through the Lonoke County collector along with the rest of the county, and the state's property tax portal lists a Lonoke County payment page. Because tax is paid in arrears, the person who owns the house on the assessment date is billed for the year, and the closing statement decides how the amount is split between buyer and seller.

Arkansas also charges a real property transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of the consideration on transfers above $100. Read the state transfer tax page for the official wording.

Camp Nelson, events and the wider county around Cabot

Cabot sits next to places with long histories. In 1862 a typhoid epidemic killed about 1,500 Confederate soldiers camped in the hills around Cabot and Austin, and in 1905 veterans moved 428 graves to the Camp Nelson Confederate Cemetery. Volunteers from Cabot began maintaining it in 1982.

The city also holds Cabotfest each October downtown and Strawberry Fest each spring, a nod to the strawberries once shipped from the area by rail. The city has 43 churches and two country clubs, Greystone on the north end and Rolling Hills in the southeast.

The county beyond town is rural. Lonoke County moved from cotton to rice after a 1904 demonstration, rice farming remains part of its economy, and waterways such as Bayou Meto and the Big Ditch run through it. Acreage and country houses outside the city limits can raise different questions than a subdivision lot inside Cabot, so tell a buyer exactly where your parcel lies.

Sellers here often have a house that needs updating, a job transfer, a rental with tenants, or an inherited house with several owners. The Air Force Base link means some owners have only weeks to move.

How far is Cabot from Little Rock?

About 22 miles southwest on the I-57 and U.S. 67 and 167 freeway. Jacksonville is 9 miles from Cabot on the same route.

They are due by October 15, with a 10 percent penalty on unpaid balances after that date. Collection starts the first business day of March, and installments are allowed under state law.

Where is Centerton, Arkansas, and how did it start?

Centerton is a city in Benton County, Arkansas, about 5 miles west of Bentonville on Arkansas Highway 102, near the center of the county. The highway runs 11 miles farther west to Decatur.

Native hunters and early settlers were drawn to natural springs here, including McKissick Spring. A church and school built along the spring were called Center Point, and Union troops camped at the spring on March 5, 1862, shortly before the Battle of Pea Ridge. The Arkansas-Oklahoma Railroad later linked Rogers and Grove, Oklahoma, through western Benton County and opened apple and strawberry orchards to new markets. The town was laid out in 1900 and renamed Centerton because Center Point was already registered in Howard County. Centerton was established as a city on September 16, 1914.

How fast has Centerton grown?

Centerton is largely a suburb of Bentonville, so its job base is the Northwest Arkansas regional economy. Between 2007 and 2013 the region had unemployment well below peer regions and the national average, and it added about 8,300 jobs, 6,100 of them in education and health. Manufacturing declined while professional, education and health care work grew. For a Centerton seller, that means buyers often come from regional employers and relocations.

  • Decatur High School is the comprehensive high school for the Decatur district.
  • Lifeway Christian School (preschool to grade 12) is based at First Baptist Church Centerton.

Zoning differs by street, so confirm the school assignment for your address before sharing it with a buyer.

How does Benton County frame the Centerton market?

Benton County had 284,333 residents in the 2020 census and an estimate of 332,554 for 2025. Bentonville is the county seat, and the county is reported to have the highest median household income in Arkansas. Walmart, agriculture (especially poultry, cattle and hogs), tourism and construction all shape its economy.

Northwest Arkansas Regional Airport lies south of Centerton, and Highway 102 is the main road through the center of the city. U.S. 62 and 71 cross the county. The county also holds Beaver Lake, Pea Ridge National Military Park and parts of the Ozark National Forest, so buyers moving to the area often compare Centerton with towns nearer those places. Be ready to explain what your location offers in terms of commute time to Bentonville, which is about 5 miles east.

Centerton shares the climate of the rest of Benton County, which has four seasons. Nearby Bentonville averages 47.33 inches of precipitation and 9.5 inches of snow a year, with a July high around 89 degrees and a January high around 46 degrees.

Benton County also sits on the Springfield Plateau, a karst landscape of springs, sinkholes and caves. In a city named for a spring, that is relevant: drainage, runoff and ground conditions around a house are worth checking. Roof condition after storms and the heating system after cold snaps are the other things buyers tend to ask about.

What permits and city rules affect selling in Centerton?

Centerton's Building Safety department issues building, plumbing, electrical, mechanical, demolition, pool and solar permits, among others, and reviews plans. It lists the Arkansas Fire Code 2021, Arkansas Plumbing Code 2018, Arkansas Fuel Gas Code 2018, the International Mechanical Code 2021 and NFPA 70 (2020) among the codes it applies.

Inspections are scheduled through an online portal at bsaonline.com, and fire inspections are handled separately by the Fire Marshal or Fire Chief. A certificate of occupancy is issued before a structure is occupied. You can email buildingsafety@centertonar.us or call 479-795-2750.

When you prepare to sell, check these items:

  • Whether a deck, shed, pool or addition has a permit on file.
  • Whether any open permit still needs a final inspection.
  • Whether your subdivision has covenants that limit changes.

How do property taxes work when selling a house in Centerton?

Because Centerton is in Benton County, the county collector bills the tax. The books open on the first business day of March, and a 10 percent penalty applies to what is unpaid after October 15. Real estate that stays unpaid also accrues interest. The county says tax statements must be mailed by July 1.

Taxes are paid one year behind, so a 2026 assessment is billed in 2027 and due October 15, 2027. The bill goes to the owner of record on January 1 of the tax year, and closing documents explain how the buyer and seller handle it. If a mortgage company receives the bill, check within 30 to 60 days that it was paid.

The Benton County assessor appraises a sold house at 20 percent of appraised value at the next assessment date after title transfers, and a new owner cannot claim an assessed-value limitation until the second assessment date after transfer. The homestead credit is up to $600 for a primary residence. The county's next reappraisal is listed as 2028. Arkansas also charges a transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transfers above $100; see the state's transfer tax page.

Where is Conway, Arkansas, and how is the city laid out?

Conway is the county seat of Faulkner County, in Central Arkansas, about 30 miles northwest of Little Rock. The city sits at 331 feet of elevation and covers roughly 46 square miles, nearly all of it land.

The town began in 1872 as "Conway Station," laid out by Asa P. Robinson, chief engineer of the Little Rock and Fort Smith Railroad. It was incorporated on October 16, 1875. The railroad still shapes the older core, although Conway has no passenger rail service today.

Interstate 40 wraps the northern and eastern edges of the city, with Conway exits numbered 124 through 132. US 64 and US 65 cross town as well. Little Rock is 30 miles away and Russellville 46, so many Conway houses are a short drive from an interstate ramp.

Lake Conway, on the city's edge, is described as the largest man-made lake built by a state game and fish commission in the country. Homes near the water draw a different crowd of buyers than homes near the campuses downtown.

The city has also seen plants come and go. The IC Corporation school bus plant closed in 2010 and moved to Tulsa, and a large facility announced by HP in 2008 for 1,200 jobs was later abandoned and is now leased by Gainwell. Westrock Coffee bought a 524,000 square foot facility in 2021, with 250 jobs expected.

An owner who has to relocate because of a layoff or a transfer is a common reason people look for a quick sale here. Stable anchors like the hospital and the university soften that risk, but they do not remove it.

How do colleges and schools affect selling a house in Conway?

Three colleges in town shape both the rental market and the pattern of home sales. The University of Central Arkansas has about 12,000 students, Hendrix College a little over 1,300, and Central Baptist College nearly 900.

Conway Public Schools serves most of the city, with about 10,000 students and 16 schools, which gives it the eighth-largest enrollment in Arkansas. Small parts of the city fall inside the Mayflower and Greenbrier districts, so check the district for a specific address before you describe the home to a buyer. Conway Christian School and St. Joseph Catholic School are the larger private options.

Landlords near campus often sell when a tenant turns over, because a vacant unit with deferred repairs is hard to show during the school year. A buyer who pays cash and takes the house as it is can fit that timeline better than a listing that waits for the next semester.

What does Conway's climate mean for the condition of a house?

Conway has a humid subtropical climate, with about 51 inches of rain a year and very little snow, around 2.3 inches. Roofs, gutters, crawlspaces and HVAC systems do most of the work here.

Temperatures have ranged from a record 115 degrees in July and August to a record low of minus 15. Average daily highs are near 72 degrees across the year, so a heat pump or air conditioner that is past its life is one of the first things a buyer inspector flags.

Severe storms are part of local history. An F4 tornado struck Conway on April 10, 1965, killing six people and injuring 200. Sellers with older roofs should keep any storm-damage paperwork, since buyers and lenders ask for it.

  • Check the roof age and any hail or wind claims before listing.
  • Look for moisture under the house after a wet spring.
  • Gather HVAC service records if you have them.

How and when are property taxes paid on a Conway house?

Faulkner County collects real estate tax between March 1 and October 15 each year, and anything paid after October 15 draws a 10% penalty. Real estate tax also accrues 10% annual interest after that date, according to the county collector.

The collector's main office is at 806 Faulkner St. in Conway, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, with a second office in Greenbrier. You can pay online, by mail or in person. Personal property tax has to be paid before or with real estate tax, so an unpaid vehicle bill can block an online real estate payment.

An owner who lives in the home can apply once for the homestead credit, worth up to $600 a year, and must reapply after a move. At closing, the title company normally settles the current year's tax between buyer and seller, so ask for the tax figures early and confirm them with the collector. State law sets the payment window in Ark. Code 26-36-201.

What does a sale cost in Conway besides taxes?

Arkansas charges a real property transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of the actual price on deeds that convey real estate. The state Department of Finance and Administration administers it, and the transfer stamp is bought at recording. Your contract states who pays it.

Other costs depend on the route you pick:

  • Listing with an agent: commission, repairs asked for after inspection, and carrying costs while the house is on the market.
  • Selling it yourself: marketing, legal paperwork and showings on your own time.
  • Cash offer: the buyer buys the house as it is, so there are no repair requests, and the closing timeline is set in the contract.

Recorded deeds in Faulkner County go through the circuit clerk, which also keeps a land records search online.

Who sells a house fast in Conway, and why?

Sellers in Conway usually have one of a few situations: an inherited house with no one to live in it, a rental with a tenant who left damage, a job move, or a mortgage that has fallen behind. Each one has a clock attached.

An inherited house needs the estate paperwork in order before anyone can sign a deed, and that process runs through the court. A house with a tax or lien problem needs payoff figures. A rental needs the tenant situation settled, since an occupied house limits what a buyer can do.

If any of these fits, the practical first step is to list the facts: who is on the title, what is owed, what condition the roof and systems are in, and when you need to close. A cash buyer can then base an offer on that list, and you can compare it with the net from a listing.

Where is Fayetteville, Arkansas, and what is the terrain like?

Fayetteville is the county seat of Washington County, in the Ozarks of Northwest Arkansas, at the edge of the Boston Mountains. The city stands at about 1,378 feet of elevation and covers roughly 55 square miles.

Settlers arrived around 1828, and the town was incorporated on November 3, 1836. The Civil War left a mark: Union forces under General Samuel Curtis occupied the town in February 1862, retreating Confederates burned their arsenal and much of the town, and the Action at Fayetteville followed on April 18, 1863.

Hilly ground matters when you sell. Slopes, steep driveways, retaining walls and older foundations on Mount Sequoyah or near the Square draw closer inspection than a flat lot would.

Walmart and J.B. Hunt are headquartered nearby, and Tyson is based in neighboring Springdale. Regional corporate jobs feed the buyer pool, while the university feeds the rental pool. Owners of student rentals often sell after a lease ends or after a long vacancy.

Local descriptions divide the city by the major roads and the campus. The areas include:

  • Uptown, near the Northwest Arkansas Mall in the north.

Wilson Park, Mount Nord and Washington-Willow are the named historic districts. A house in one of them can come with design expectations from neighbors and the city, so ask the planning office before you plan exterior changes you want to make before a sale.

Which school district serves Fayetteville homes?

Fayetteville Public Schools serves most of the city. The district was established in 1871 and runs eight elementary schools, four intermediate schools, two special schools and Fayetteville High School.

Buyers with children often check attendance zones before they make an offer, so write down the zoned schools for your address and confirm them with the district. A few edges of the city may sit in other districts, which the district office can confirm.

Interstate 49, which carries US 71, is the city's main through route. It was formerly I-540, and the redesignation to I-49 was approved on March 28, 2014. College Avenue, the old US 71B, remains a commercial spine.

The Razorback Greenway is a 36-mile, mostly off-road shared-use trail that links Fayetteville with Bella Vista through Johnson, Springdale, Lowell, Bentonville and Rogers. Homes with easy trail access often highlight it in listings.

Northwest Arkansas National Airport, which opened in 1998, is about 17 miles northwest of the city. Drake Field, the municipal airport, handles general aviation and many Razorback team charters.

July highs average near 89 degrees and January lows near 27, and the city sees about 47 inches of precipitation a year with an average of 3.3 snowy days.

Extremes are larger than the averages. The city's record high is 111 degrees, set on July 14, 1954, and its record low is minus 24 on February 12, 1899. Pipes in unheated crawlspaces and older roofs are the usual trouble spots after a hard winter.

Before a sale, buyers tend to ask about the age of the roof, the HVAC system and the water heater, so have receipts ready.

What are Fayetteville's short-term rental rules?

Applicants needed a business license, a building safety inspection, proof of ownership, an insurance review, sales tax filings and a landlord registry listing. In January 2022 the city had received 376 applications and approved 177, and officials estimated 500 to 600 rentals operated in the city. The council also widened the zones where they are allowed.

If you own a rental that has a permit, ask the planning office whether it transfers to a new owner before you promise it to a buyer.

How do property taxes work for a Fayetteville seller?

Washington County bills real estate tax, due by October 15 each year. Payments after that date draw a 10% penalty, and real estate also accrues 10% annual interest, according to the county collector.

You can pay online by credit card, which carries a processing fee, in person, or by mail using the instructions on your annual statement. For statement questions the collector lists 479-444-1526. The collector's page does not explain proration at a sale, so ask the title company how the current year's tax will be divided at closing.

A cash sale fits Fayetteville owners who want certainty more than the highest price on a listing. Typical cases include a house that needs work the owner cannot fund, an inherited property in another owner's name, a landlord leaving the rental business, or a move that has a firm date.

Where is Fort Smith, Arkansas, and why does the border matter?

Fort Smith sits on the Oklahoma line in western Arkansas, where the Arkansas and Poteau rivers meet at a spot called Belle Point. It is a seat of Sebastian County, one of two in the county, and stands at about 463 feet of elevation.

Fort Chaffee, east of the city, was established in 1941 and later served as a resettlement center for Vietnamese refugees in 1975. The former military land now includes the Chaffee Crossing area, a newer economic zone in east Fort Smith.

Miss Laura's Social Club, a former brothel and the only remaining building from the area known as the Row, is also on the Register.

Judge Parker sentenced 160 people to death during his tenure, and 79 were executed. Deputy marshal Bass Reeves worked with the court and is remembered as one of the first African American lawmen west of the Mississippi.

Fort Smith has real flood history. In May 2019 the Arkansas River reached record levels, and flows at Trimble Lock and Dam near the city rose from 170,000 cubic feet per second on May 22 to more than 500,000 across the river soon after.

The Red Cross opened a shelter in Fort Smith on May 24, and as many as 200 people evacuated the city by May 25. About 545 homes in Sebastian County were eventually affected. Floodwater also backed up into Massard Creek, and Sebastian County was added to the federal disaster declaration.

A house that took on water, or sits near the river, needs documentation before a sale. Gather any insurance claim, repair invoices and permit records. A buyer will ask whether the house is in a mapped flood zone, and you can look up your address on the FEMA flood map service.

What does weather mean for houses in Fort Smith?

Fort Smith has a humid subtropical climate with a January mean of 40.4 degrees and a July mean of 83.1 degrees. It averages 47.34 inches of precipitation and 2.9 inches of snow a year.

The record high is 115 degrees, set on August 3, 2011, and the record low is minus 15 on February 12, 1899. Tornadoes have hit the city three times in major form, in 1898, 1927 and 1996. The 1898 storm killed more than fifty residents, and the 1996 storm killed four people in Fort Smith and Van Buren.

  • Ask a roofer to check shingles and flashing after any hail season.
  • Keep records of storm repairs and insurance payouts.
  • Check that the crawlspace drains and the sump, if there is one, work.

Which schools, roads and airport serve Fort Smith?

The Fort Smith School District operates 26 schools, including two high schools, four middle schools and 19 elementary schools, plus one alternative school. Its enrollment exceeded 14,748 in 2019 to 2020. The University of Arkansas at Fort Smith joined the university system on January 1, 2002, and the Arkansas College of Osteopathic Medicine welcomed its first class in August 2017.

The city lies just southwest of where I-40 and I-49 intersect, and US 64, US 71 and US 271 also serve it. Fort Smith Regional Airport has commercial service to Dallas/Fort Worth. The Arkansas River carries barge traffic through the Port of Fort Smith as part of the McClellan-Kerr Navigation System.

Transport and logistics jobs, including ArcBest, mean many households here have work that depends on highways and freight.

How are Fort Smith property taxes handled when you sell?

Sebastian County collects real estate tax from March 1 through October 15, and anything unpaid after October 15 is delinquent with a 10% penalty. Personal property can be assessed from January 1 through May 31, and after that the state adds a 10% penalty that cannot be removed.

Requests to correct assessment information and appeals to the Equalization Board are due the third Monday in August. Homestead credit applications for a primary residence are due October 15. Homeowners 65 or older, or disabled, can ask to have the property value frozen on a principal residence. City liens must be paid before or with taxes, so a lien on your house can hold up a payment.

Arkansas also taxes the deed itself at $3.30 per $1,000 of the sale price.

When does a cash sale make sense in Fort Smith?

Cash sales tend to suit homes that have flood history, deferred roof or foundation work, a probate case, or a tenant in place. A traditional buyer's lender will order an appraisal and may require repairs, and that can fall apart on an older or damaged house.

Collect your deed, a mortgage payoff statement, any lien information and recent tax bills. With those in hand you can compare a cash offer, a listing, and a sale by owner on cost and time.

Is Fort Smith in a flood zone?

Parts of it are. The Arkansas River reached record levels in 2019 and about 545 homes in Sebastian County were affected. Check any address on the FEMA flood map service.

When are Sebastian County property taxes due?

Between March 1 and October 15. After October 15 the collector adds a 10% penalty.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Sebastian County?

Corrections and Equalization Board appeals are due the third Monday in August, per the county.

What is the real property transfer tax in Arkansas?

$3.30 per $1,000 of the actual price on deeds that convey real estate, administered by the state Department of Finance and Administration.

Can I sell a Fort Smith house that had flood damage?

Yes. Provide repair and insurance records if you have them, and a cash buyer can take the house in its current condition.

Are veterans or seniors eligible for any Sebastian County tax relief?

Yes. Homeowners 65 or older, or disabled, can request a value freeze on a principal residence, and 100% service-connected disabled veterans must submit a VA letter by October 15 each year, according to the county.

Where is Hot Springs, Arkansas, and what sets it apart?

The city takes its name from 47 springs on the western slope of Hot Springs Mountain. About a million gallons a day flow at 143 degrees Fahrenheit, and radiocarbon dating shows the water fell as rain roughly 4,400 years earlier. Congress protected the area in 1832 by creating the Hot Springs Reservation, which was renamed Hot Springs National Park in 1921.

A short history of Hot Springs for homeowners

Hot Springs became the county seat of the newly formed Garland County in 1873, and a narrow-gauge railroad from Malvern reached the city in 1875, the year the first Arlington Hotel opened. In 1886 the Chicago White Stockings brought major league baseball to town, and the city is credited as a birthplace of spring training.

The Assemblies of God was formed here in 1914. In 1960 the Army and Navy Hospital closed and the grounds were sold to the state of Arkansas for one dollar. The area is now a historic district of 31 buildings.

Why this matters to a seller: a city built around spas and hotels has many older and unusual buildings, including thirteen hotels and eight motor courts on the National Register. Houses with odd layouts or conversion histories need clear records of what has been permitted.

How does tourism shape the Hot Springs economy and housing?

Tourism is the main economic driver in Hot Springs. Visitors come for Bathhouse Row, the thermal waters, Oaklawn Park, Magic Springs and the lakes.

  • Oaklawn Park has been a thoroughbred racetrack since 1904.
  • The Hot Springs Music Festival and the Documentary Film Festival draw seasonal crowds.
  • Hot Springs Mountain Tower, built in 1982, stands 216 feet tall.

Seasonal demand affects how long a house takes to sell and which buyers look at it. A property near downtown can appeal to someone who wants to rent it to visitors, while one in a quiet part of town fits a primary residence buyer better. Hot Springs has not always been quiet: from 1927 to 1947 it was a gambling center with no fewer than ten major casinos, and gambling was closed in 1967.

What are the short-term rental rules in Hot Springs?

Hot Springs regulates short-term rentals through business licenses and zoning. The city defines them as accommodations offered for periods under 30 days, and its board adopted the first ordinance by a 6 to 1 vote in 2021.

As reported in January 2022, the city capped licenses at 500 in residential zones, and 325 had been issued before new applications were paused. Rentals in residential zones needed a special use permit, with appeals going to the Board of Zoning Adjustment. Maximum overnight occupancy is two per bedroom plus two, and the annual license fee was $50 per maximum occupant, so a three-bedroom rental allowing eight people pays $400.

Rules and caps may have changed since then, so call the city before you tell a buyer that a license comes with the house. A house that lost its license or never had one can still sell, but the buyer will price in that risk.

  • Quapaw-Prospect Historic District: 233 structures.

  • Whittington Park Historic District: 60 single-family houses and ten other structures.
  • Army and Navy General Hospital Historic District: 31 buildings.

A house in or beside one of these districts may face limits on exterior changes. Ask the city planning office before you start work you want to finish before selling.

The city has burned twice in major fires. A March 1878 fire left more than 1,000 people homeless, and the 1913 "Black Friday" fire damaged about 60 blocks. Many older homes were rebuilt after those fires, so wiring and plumbing age is worth checking.

What does the climate mean for a Hot Springs house?

Hot Springs is hot and wet, with a July average high of 93.1 degrees and annual precipitation of 57.96 inches over roughly 110 days. May is the wettest month at 6.51 inches, and snow averages about 1.1 inches a year.

The record high is 115 degrees, set in 1936 and 1986, and the record low is minus 11, set in 1930. Roofs, air conditioning and drainage take the most wear, and the hilly setting means water runoff near foundations deserves attention.

  • Test the air conditioning before listing.
  • Check gutters and grading around the foundation.
  • Look for staining on ceilings after heavy spring rain.

Five public school districts serve the city: Hot Springs, Lakeside, Cutter-Morning Star, Fountain Lake and Lake Hamilton. Hot Springs School District covers most of the city, so your address decides which district your buyer's children will attend. National Park College is also in town.

US 70 and US 270 bypass downtown to the south on the Martin Luther King Jr. Expressway, and US 70 Business and US 270 Business run through the center. Arkansas Highway 7 runs through downtown, 71 miles north to Russellville and 35 miles south to Arkadelphia. Interstate 30 passes southeast of the city, with the closest access 17 miles away via US 270.

Lake Hamilton and Lake Catherine lie south of the city on the Ouachita River. Lake Catherine State Park was created in 1935, and Carpenter Dam, which formed Lake Hamilton, is on the National Register.

How are property taxes and transfer costs handled in Hot Springs?

Garland County collects real estate tax from the first business day of March through October 15, and unpaid tax after that date is delinquent with a 10% penalty under state law. Arkansas also charges $3.30 per $1,000 of the price on deeds that convey real estate, with the state's Miscellaneous Tax Section handling transfer stamps. Ask the title company to confirm who pays in your contract and what the final figure will be.

Where is Paragould, and how is the city laid out?

Paragould is the county seat of Greene County in northeastern Arkansas, and it is the 15th-largest city in the state. It sits on the eastern edge of Crowley's Ridge, a line of higher ground that rises out of the flat Arkansas Delta.

The city covers a little over 32 square miles, and its elevation is about 289 feet. U.S. 412 and U.S. 49 cross just west of downtown. Highway 412 runs about 9 miles east to the Missouri line at the St. Francis River, and U.S. 49 runs roughly 20 miles southwest to Jonesboro. Memphis is the nearest major city, about 82 miles to the southeast.

For a seller, the practical point is access. Two federal routes and a short drive to Jonesboro and the Missouri line make Paragould workable for commuters, and that is worth mentioning to any buyer.

How did Paragould get its name and start growing?

Paragould exists because two railroads crossed here in 1882: the Texas & St. Louis Railway, later the Cotton Belt, and the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern, later the Missouri Pacific. The name joins the surnames of two railroad figures, J. W. Paramore and Jay Gould, and the town is believed to be the only one with that name anywhere.

In 1888 the town became the starting point of the Paragould and Buffalo Island Railway, which later reached Blytheville. Greene County moved its seat to Paragould in 1883, and the county courthouse built in 1888 still stands downtown.

A town that dates to the 1880s has houses of many ages. When we look at an older Paragould house, the questions are usually about the roof, the foundation, the electrical panel and the plumbing, since those are the systems that age first.

What do Paragould's weather numbers mean for a house?

Paragould has a humid subtropical climate, which means hot, wet summers and short, mild winters. The 1991 to 2020 normals show a July mean daily high of 89.8 degrees and a January mean daily high of 45.7 degrees.

The city averages 51.74 inches of precipitation a year across about 115 days, and only about 2.5 inches of snow. Recorded extremes run from 106 degrees to minus 14 degrees.

  • Air conditioning does most of the work from late spring into early fall, so the age of the condenser and ductwork is a real value item.
  • Fifty-plus inches of rain a year puts pressure on roofs, gutters, grading and crawl space vents.
  • Occasional hard freezes make exposed pipes and old water heaters a repair risk.

Deferred maintenance in any of these systems is the usual reason a Paragould owner decides to sell as-is instead of paying for repairs first.

The city grew by about 3,400 people in the 2010s, which is steady growth for a Delta-region county seat. Greene County itself is 580 square miles and borders Clay, Craighead, Lawrence and Randolph counties in Arkansas, plus Dunklin County, Missouri.

Which utilities and schools serve a Paragould home?

Paragould Light, Water and Cable, a municipally owned utility, provides electric service inside the city, along with water from its own wells, sewer treatment and cable broadband. A fiber internet build is also under way in phases. Natural gas comes from CenterPoint Energy. Outside the city limits, Craighead Electric or Entergy Arkansas serve parts of Greene County, and rural water associations cover some areas.

That split matters when a seller lists a house just outside town. Buyers should confirm which provider serves the address, because a rural address may not have city water or sewer at all.

Two public districts serve the area: the Paragould School District, formed in 1985 by merging with Oak Grove and renamed in 1997, and the Greene County Tech School District. Private options include Crowley's Ridge Academy and St. Mary's Catholic School. Higher education includes Crowley's Ridge College and a Black River Technical College campus. A Paragould address does not always tell you which district a home is in, so sellers should check the district map before advertising a school.

How do property taxes work when a Paragould house sells?

Greene County bills Paragould real estate tax, and the county collector is at 320 West Court Street in Paragould. The collector's page says taxes become payable on March 1, when the books open, and the deadline to pay without penalty is October 15. Real estate left unpaid after that date carries a 10% penalty plus a daily fee. The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, and you can pay online, by phone or at the counter.

The state sets the rules for how the county values a house. According to the Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration, properties are reappraised every 3, 4 or 5 years. If you disagree with a value, start with the county assessor, because simple errors in square footage or room counts can often be fixed without a hearing. For a formal appeal, the deadline to schedule a hearing with the County Board of Equalization is the third Monday in August.

  • The homestead tax credit is up to $500 a year, rising to up to $600 beginning with 2026 tax bills.
  • Under Amendment 79, a homestead's taxable value can rise no more than 5% a year, and other real property is limited to 10% a year.
  • The caps do not apply to new construction or substantial improvements that add at least 25% to value.

A buyer does not inherit a seller's age 65 or disability freeze, so an older owner with a low taxable value should expect the next owner's bill to look different.

What does Arkansas require at a Paragould closing?

Arkansas charges a real estate transfer tax of $3.30 for every $1,000 of actual consideration on deeds over $100, and the state sells the tax as a stamp that is purchased at recording. The statute text on Justia lists a base rate of $1.10 per $1,000 and an additional $2.20 per $1,000 that it says is to be paid by the purchaser, so who pays what is something to settle in the contract.

Arkansas does not require every seller to disclose every known defect. The Arkansas Real Estate Commission says the Seller Property Disclosure form from the Arkansas Realtors Association is not legally mandated, although Realtors encourage sellers to complete it. If no agent is involved, disclosure duties come from the contract the two sides sign.

In practice, a Paragould seller should still write down known problems such as roof leaks, past water in the crawl space or a failed inspection. A clear list protects the seller later and speeds up a cash sale.

What are the realistic ways to sell a Paragould house?

A Paragould owner has three paths: list with an agent, sell privately, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases the house as it stands. Each one trades time, cost and certainty differently.

  • Listing with an agent: exposure to financed buyers, but showings, repairs requested after inspection, appraisal timing and a commission to pay.
  • Selling privately: no commission, but you handle pricing, paperwork, the transfer stamp and any buyer questions yourself.
  • Cash sale: an as-is purchase with no financing contingency, which suits inherited houses, tenant-occupied houses and homes that need work.

Whichever route you choose, gather the last tax statement, any utility account details from Paragould Light, Water and Cable, and the deed before you talk to a buyer. Those three items answer most early questions.

More questions about Paragould, AR

How many people live in Paragould?

The Census Bureau estimates 31,135 residents as of July 1, 2025. The city counted 29,537 people in the 2020 census and 26,113 in 2010.

When are Greene County property taxes due?

Greene County taxes can be paid starting March 1, and they are due without penalty by October 15. Real estate taxes left unpaid after that date carry a 10% penalty plus a daily fee, according to the county collector.

Who provides electricity and water in Paragould?

Paragould Light, Water and Cable provides electricity, water, sewer and cable broadband inside city limits. CenterPoint Energy supplies natural gas, and rural addresses may be served by Craighead Electric, Entergy Arkansas or a rural water association.

Do Arkansas sellers have to fill out a disclosure form?

No state law requires every seller to complete a disclosure form. The Arkansas Realtors Association form is encouraged but not mandatory, and sellers who skip it can still be held to the terms of the sale contract.

Can I sell a Paragould house that needs repairs?

Yes. You can list it, sell it yourself or sell it as-is to a cash buyer. Repairs only need to be done if a financed buyer's lender or inspection requires them.

Where is Pine Bluff and what is the area like?

Pine Bluff is the seat of Jefferson County in southeast Arkansas, on the Arkansas River in the Delta lowlands. The county sits about 43 miles southeast of Little Rock and borders Lonoke, Arkansas, Lincoln, Cleveland, Grant and Pulaski counties.

The city covers roughly 46 square miles at an elevation of 226 feet, and the terrain is flat farmland and river bottom. Water shapes the map: the Arkansas River, Lake Pine Bluff, Lake Langhofer at the slack water harbor, and Bayou Bartholomew on the western edge, where the Delta gives way to the Timberlands.

The city runs on a mayor-council system with an eight-member council, two members from each of four wards. A seller who needs to deal with the city on a permit or a code notice will be working with that government rather than the county, so it helps to know which office sent a letter.

How did Pine Bluff develop?

Pine Bluff began as a river settlement after the flood of 1819 and was officially named by the county court on October 16, 1832. It was incorporated on January 8, 1839, and the first railroad arrived in December 1873.

Cotton and river trade made it the third-largest city in Arkansas by 1890. Jefferson County produced 55,120 bales of cotton in 1886, the most of any county in the state. Victorian-style houses were built west of Main Street as personal fortunes grew from the 1870s.

The Army broke ground on the Pine Bluff Arsenal on December 2, 1941, on about 15,000 acres north of the city. Later, a kraft paper mill was announced in 1957, and the Port of Pine Bluff anchors the Harbor Industrial District along the river.

A city that has been building since the 1830s has houses from many eras. A Victorian-era house west of Main Street and a newer house on the edge of town raise different repair questions, and a cash buyer prices them separately.

Three public districts serve the city: Pine Bluff, Watson Chapel and White Hall. The Dollarway School District merged into Pine Bluff on July 1, 2021, and Dollarway High School closed in 2023. Because a street can sit in any of these districts, a seller should confirm the district of the address before quoting it.

Interstate 530 is the southern bypass, and U.S. 63, 65, 79, 270 and 425 also run through the area, along with Arkansas Highways 15, 54, 81, 190 and 365. Grider Field is a general airport about 4 miles southeast of town, and Clinton National in Little Rock handles most commercial flights. Pine Bluff Transit runs six routes, and Union Pacific provides freight rail.

Dollarway Road, completed in 1914, was the longest continuous stretch of concrete road in the country at that time.

What does Pine Bluff's flood history mean for a house?

Pine Bluff's flat river-delta location means flood history is a fair question for any buyer. The Great Flood of 1927 flooded most of northern and southeastern Jefferson County and broke levees, and the 1933 Mississippi River flood displaced residents who relocated to Pine Bluff.

The Army Corps of Engineers built a levee to keep the river's main channel near the city, and the channel eventually shifted away and left an oxbow that became Lake Pine Bluff. A levee system now runs 380 miles from Pine Bluff to Venice, Louisiana.

The city averages about 53.6 inches of rain a year over roughly 97 days, with a mean daily high of 73.2 degrees and a record high of 112. Humidity, heat and heavy rain make roof condition, drainage and crawl space moisture the main issues in an older house here. Check FEMA's flood map for the specific address before a sale, because the ground you stand on matters more than the city name.

How does Jefferson County handle property tax?

The Jefferson County Tax Collector, at 101 West Barraque in Pine Bluff, collects property and real estate taxes, municipal liens and business personal property tax. Its filing season runs from March 1 to October 15 each year, and the office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 5:00 pm. The phone number is 870-541-5313.

State rules apply on top of that. The state reappraises property every 3, 4 or 5 years, and the deadline to schedule a hearing with the County Board of Equalization is the third Monday in August. Homestead owners can claim a credit of up to $500 a year, rising to up to $600 with 2026 tax bills, and the taxable value of a homestead cannot rise more than 5% a year under Amendment 79.

Taxes that go unpaid can lead to a sale by the Commissioner of State Lands. In 2023 that office sold just over 200 Jefferson County properties, most for under $500, and as of October 28, 2024, 40 Pine Bluff properties were offered at an online auction after failing to sell at the first one. If you owe back taxes on a house you want to sell, start with the collector before the delinquency grows.

What vacant-property and code issues do Pine Bluff sellers face?

Pine Bluff is one of three Delta cities that worked with Community Progress for about 18 months on strategies for vacant, abandoned and deteriorated properties, and Jefferson County is among the 20 Arkansas counties with the highest residential vacancy rates.

It can be certified for the Commissioner of State Lands and sold at the annual sale. Properties that do not sell move to a post-auction list.

The Arkansas River Valley lies in the south, with farmland and towns, while the Ozarks, including part of the Boston Mountains, cover nearly two-thirds of the county to the north. Russellville won the Pope County seat in a March 19, 1887 election, beating Atkins by 128 votes out of 2,670 cast. Dover had been the seat since 1841.

The first house was a hand-hewn log house built in 1834 by J. C. Holledger and bought in 1835 by Dr. Thomas Russell, for whom the town was named around 1842. Incorporation came on June 7, 1870, and railroad construction in the early 1870s took the town from about 240 residents in 1870 to about 800 by 1876.

A fire on January 16, 1906 destroyed nearly half of the downtown business district, including 23 buildings. Interstate 40 construction began in 1956 and spurred growth, and a dam completed in 1965 created Lake Dardanelle.

Russellville's economy rests on manufacturing, a nuclear plant, a university and a lake. About 50 manufacturing plants employ more than 8,300 people, and more than ten divisions of Fortune 500 companies have facilities in the city.
